# Authoring guide set: full content

> Every guide section in one file, in order. Each chunk starts with a comment line `<!-- chunk: id | source | title | rules -->`. Prefer the single chunk files (chunks/index.json) when you only need one topic.

<!-- chunk: readme--introduction | source: README.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# Authoring Guide Set for IFC Buildings, Materials and Furniture

Version 2.5.0 (2026-10-30). Application-neutral guides, rules, checkers and examples for people and software agents who create
digital buildings, finishes, wall coverings and furniture in the IFC building-data format, so that their work can be used by many
different programs. Start with [ABOUT.md](ABOUT.md): what this is, who it is for, and how a consumer adopts it.

In these guides **the consumer** is whatever program or person receives your delivery (a viewer, a simulator, a game runtime, a BIM
tool, an archive). **A profile** is the small JSON file a consumer publishes with its numbers and conventions; if you have none, use
`profiles/default.json`. Everything else is in these guides.

---

<!-- chunk: readme--core-and-profile | source: README.md | title: Core and profile | rules: - -->
## Core and profile

* **Core rules** say what is good practice for any consumer and what goes wrong for any consumer if you ignore it.
* **Profile parameters** hold everything numeric or consumer-specific: size and triangle limits, identifier lengths, clearances,
  property names, whether room identifiers are mandatory, and which optional extensions apply. See
  [07-profile-parameters.md](07-profile-parameters.md).
* **Extensions** (`walkability`, `luminaires`, `signboards`, `furnitureCollision`, `terrain`) are optional rule groups a profile switches on.

Check anything against a profile: `python3 tools/check_all.py PATH --profile consumer.json --json`. Reports name the profile used.

---

<!-- chunk: readme--for-agents | source: README.md | title: For agents | rules: - -->
## For agents

The set is also written to be read and run by software agents of any kind. Static files only; no service is needed.

| File | Use |
|---|---|
| [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) | short entry point: what the set is, commands, working rules |
| `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` | index of the set, and all content in marked chunks |
| `skills/` | six skills (orient, author-building, decorate-interior, author-furniture-library, accept-and-package-delivery, submit-delivery), each with a short `SKILL.md` and on-demand `references/` |
| `rules.json` | all rules with level, applies_to, parameters, extension, how to check, fix hint, examples |
| [REPAIR-LOOP.md](REPAIR-LOOP.md) | run, read findings, fix, rerun until no REQUIRED finding remains |
| `profiles/` | the profile schema, the default profile, and an example of a strict consumer profile |
| `chunks/`, `MANIFEST.json` | the guides in pieces of about 1,500 tokens or less; every file with purpose and tags |
| `schemas/` | JSON Schemas: profile, rules, checker report, delivery manifest, submission block, proof manifest, catalogue, material library, furniture item, building summary, finish schedule |

<!-- chunk: readme--the-five-guides | source: README.md | title: The five guides | rules: - -->
## The five guides

| # | File | Who it is for | What it settles |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [01-builders-and-architects-guide.md](01-builders-and-architects-guide.md) | architects, builders, modellers | file and schema, units, axes, levels, rooms, walls, floors, stairs, doors, openings, identifiers, property sets, geometry hygiene, optional lighting and signs |
| 2 | [02-interior-decorators-guide.md](02-interior-decorators-guide.md) | decorators, material and texture authors | finishes, coverings, floors and ceilings, colour keys, finish schedule, texture sets, material libraries |
| 3 | [03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md](03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md) | furniture and fixture designers | item library format, pivots, dimensions, anchors, clearances, collision, variants, instancing |
| 4 | [04-delivery-and-acceptance-guide.md](04-delivery-and-acceptance-guide.md) | everyone who sends or receives | package layout, manifest with hashes, versions, provenance and licences, checklist, acceptance checks, outcomes |
| 5 | [05-worked-example.md](05-worked-example.md) | everyone | one room with a door, a window, a table, a wall covering and a light, with a generator script and checker |

<!-- chunk: readme--environment-quality-and-remote-work | source: README.md | title: Environment quality and remote work | rules: - -->
## Environment quality and remote work

Follow [Environment review and asynchronous handoff](09-environment-review-and-handoff.md) for source-to-consumer visual checks, all-room circulation, materials/UVs, lighting, revision invalidation and resumable contributor evidence. Start a handoff with `templates/environment-handoff.template.json`. Technical validation and visual acceptance remain separate decisions.

---

<!-- chunk: readme--submissions | source: README.md | title: Submissions | rules: - -->
## Submissions

The same repository takes outside deliveries as pull requests from forks: fork it, build the delivery in a branch of your fork under
`deliveries/<slug>/`, open a pull request against `main`. Acceptance is a merge to `main`; `tools/ingest.py` then turns the merged delivery into
component assets and a neutral catalogue. See [08-submissions-and-ingest.md](08-submissions-and-ingest.md) and
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Deliveries are not part of the guide set and are not in its hand-over files.

Also: [06-rules-index.md](06-rules-index.md) (every rule in one table, with counts), [07-profile-parameters.md](07-profile-parameters.md), [08-submissions-and-ingest.md](08-submissions-and-ingest.md),
[templates/](templates/) (starting files), [tools/](tools/) (scripts), [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md), [VERSIONING.md](VERSIONING.md),
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), [LICENSE.md](LICENSE.md).

---

<!-- chunk: readme--how-rules-are-written | source: README.md | title: How rules are written | rules: B-12,B-90 -->
## How rules are written

> **B-12 · REQUIRED** - The statement.
>
> **B-90 · REQUIRED · luminaires** - A statement that applies only in the named extension.

* **REQUIRED** means that without it a consumer is likely to refuse the file, lose the element, or read it wrongly, or (guide 4) that
  the delivery process requires it. A delivery that breaks a REQUIRED rule is sent back.
* **RECOMMENDED** means good practice that prevents a defect often seen or keeps work portable. A delivery that ignores it is accepted if
  everything REQUIRED passes, but the reviewer may ask for revision.
* The level shown is the **default**. A profile can raise, lower or switch off any rule (`ruleLevels`); `rules.json` and the checkers use
  the profile's level.
* Numbers are never in a rule's text as a requirement: they are profile parameters, written in `backticks` (`limits.maxTriangles`).

Identifier letters: **B** builders and architects, **D** decorators, **F** furniture and fixtures, **X** delivery and acceptance.
Numbers are never reused; a retired rule keeps its number.

---

<!-- chunk: readme--reading-order | source: README.md | title: Reading order | rules: - -->
## Reading order

1. [ABOUT.md](ABOUT.md), then the vocabulary and profile sections of guide 1 (sections 1 and 2).
2. The guide for your role (1, 2 or 3).
3. Guide 4 before you package anything.
4. Guide 5 once, even if you only make furniture.

---

<!-- chunk: readme--words-used-in-a-fixed-sense | source: README.md | title: Words used in a fixed sense | rules: - -->
## Words used in a fixed sense

| Word | Meaning here |
|---|---|
| consumer | the program or person that receives and uses your delivery |
| profile | a consumer's published parameters (`profiles/profile.schema.json`) |
| delivery | everything you submit for one assignment (files, manifest, notes) |
| level | one horizontal floor of a building (an `IfcBuildingStorey`) |
| room | a named area with a floor, modelled as an `IfcSpace` (the IFC entity name; it always means "room or zone") |
| zone | a named volume that is data only (`IfcSpatialZone`) |
| volume | any three-dimensional extent |
| finish | the look of a surface (colour, texture, gloss) |
| item | one piece of furniture, fixture or accent |
| declaration property | a named property this set asks you to write; a profile can rename it |
| extension | an optional group of rules a profile switches on |

<!-- chunk: readme--hand-over-files | source: README.md | title: Hand-over files | rules: - -->
## Hand-over files

[dist/](dist/) holds the single-file versions:

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `builders-guide-2.5.0.pdf` | all guides, the worked example, the submissions page and the rules index in one document |
| `builders-guide-2.5.0.html` | the same, as one web page |
| `builders-guide-2.5.0.zip` | the whole set, with `MANIFEST.sha256` |
| `SHA256SUMS.txt`, `builders-guide-2.5.0.zip.sha256` | SHA-256 of the three files above |

`MANIFEST.sha256` lists the SHA-256 of every other file in the set (`sha256sum -c MANIFEST.sha256`); `MANIFEST.json` describes the same files
with purpose and tags. `tools/build_dist.py` rebuilds all of this.

---

<!-- chunk: readme--what-this-set-does-not-cover | source: README.md | title: What this set does not cover | rules: - -->
## What this set does not cover

* Structural, mechanical or electrical design content, and any simulation of how things move or work.
* Terrain. Ground relief is not carried in IFC here; a profile may say how it is supplied.
* Commercial terms between sender and receiver.

<!-- chunk: about--introduction | source: ABOUT.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# About this set

---

<!-- chunk: about--what-it-is | source: ABOUT.md | title: What it is | rules: - -->
## What it is

A set of plain-language guides, rules, checkers and examples for making **IFC** files (the building-data format published by
buildingSMART International) that work in many different programs: viewers, simulators, game runtimes, BIM tools and archives. It
covers buildings, finishes (materials and wall coverings), furniture libraries, and the packaging and acceptance of deliveries.

It is **independent**. It is not endorsed by, affiliated with or certified by buildingSMART International or any standards body, and it
claims no conformance to any standard. The IFC specification itself is published by buildingSMART International
(https://www.buildingsmart.org/standards/bsi-standards/industry-foundation-classes/); this set is practical advice on top of it.

---

<!-- chunk: about--who-it-is-for | source: ABOUT.md | title: Who it is for | rules: - -->
## Who it is for

* **Authors**: architects, modellers, interior decorators, furniture designers, and the software agents that do their work, who want
  their files to survive contact with other people's tools.
* **Consumers**: anyone who receives IFC deliveries and wants authors to build to their needs without a meeting.
* **Reviewers and archivists**: people who check, accept or return deliveries and want findings that point at exact elements.

---

<!-- chunk: about--how-it-is-organised | source: ABOUT.md | title: How it is organised | rules: - -->
## How it is organised

The set separates **core practice** from **consumer parameters**.

* **Core** is what is good practice for any consumer: a declared unit, a stated frame, levels, rooms with real floors, doors that
  fill openings, unique identifiers, honest materials, a manifest with hashes and licences. Core rules say *what goes wrong for any
  consumer* if you ignore them.
* **Parameters** are everything numeric or consumer-specific: size and triangle limits, identifier lengths, clearance values, whether
  room identifiers are mandatory, which optional extensions apply. They live in a **profile**, a small JSON file
  (`profiles/profile.schema.json`). `profiles/default.json` has publicly defensible defaults; `profiles/example-strict.json` shows a
  constrained consumer. Rules in `rules.json` name the parameters they use.
* A **consumer profile** is simply a profile a consumer publishes. Authors and agents build to it and check against it:
  `python3 tools/check_all.py PATH --profile consumer.json --json`. Reports state which profile they used.

---

<!-- chunk: about--how-a-consumer-adopts-it | source: ABOUT.md | title: How a consumer adopts it | rules: - -->
## How a consumer adopts it

1. Copy `profiles/default.json` to `my-consumer.json`; set `name` and `version`.
2. Change the numbers that differ for you: `limits`, `budgets`, `identifiers`, `geometry`, `frame`, `buildVolume`, `keepOut`.
3. If your reader looks for particular property names or values, list them in `propertyNames` and `propertyValues`. Authors keep the
   neutral names; `python3 tools/map_properties.py in.ifc out.ifc --mapping my-consumer.json` renames them for you.
4. Make rules stricter (or switch them off) in `ruleLevels`; for example make `B-26` (room identifiers) `required`.
5. Switch on the extensions you implement: `walkability`, `luminaires`, `signboards`, `furnitureCollision`, `terrain`.
6. Validate the file against `profiles/profile.schema.json` and publish it at a stable address. Tell authors its name and version.
7. When you receive a delivery, run `check_all.py` with your profile; send findings back as they are (rule, element, fix hint).

---

<!-- chunk: about--submissions | source: ABOUT.md | title: Submissions | rules: - -->
## Submissions

The repository that holds this set also takes outside **deliveries** (buildings, interiors, furniture, materials, fixtures, hardware). A
contributor forks the repository, builds the delivery in a branch of the fork under `deliveries/<slug>/`, and opens a pull request against
`main`. A workflow checks it; a maintainer reviews it; a merge to `main` is the acceptance. A separate tool, `tools/ingest.py`, then turns a merged
delivery into content-addressed component assets and a neutral catalogue, without uploading anything. Deliveries are not part of the guide set
and are left out of the hand-over files. See `08-submissions-and-ingest.md`.

Every delivery also carries **proofs**: binary glTF (GLB) exports of the model and its components, a validation report, and a standard set of
rendered pictures (a plan per level, interior and exterior views, a contact sheet per component), all drawn headlessly and reproducibly from the GLB
files and tied together by a manifest of hashes, so that a reviewer or a catalogue can see the work without opening an IFC program.

---

<!-- chunk: about--what-it-does-not-do | source: ABOUT.md | title: What it does not do | rules: - -->
## What it does not do

It does not define a new standard, certify anything, simulate physical behaviour, or replace the IFC documentation. Static files
only: nothing here needs a network or a service.

See [README.md](README.md) for the index, [VERSIONING.md](VERSIONING.md) for how the set changes, and
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) to propose changes.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--introduction | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# Guide 1: Builder's and Architect's Guide

For architects, builders and modellers who deliver buildings, public areas and their fittings as IFC files that many
different consumers (viewers, simulators, game runtimes, BIM tools, archives) can open and use.

Rule levels and the profile mechanism are explained in the [README](README.md). Every number that depends on a consumer is
a **profile parameter**, written in `backticks` like `limits.maxTriangles`; its default is in `profiles/default.json` and the
full list is in [07-profile-parameters.md](07-profile-parameters.md).

---

<!-- chunk: g1--1-vocabulary | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 1. Vocabulary | rules: - -->
## 1. Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| consumer | any program or person that receives your delivery and uses it: a viewer, a simulator, a game runtime, a BIM tool, an archive |
| profile | the JSON file a consumer publishes with its parameters (limits, identifier rules, optional extensions); the default profile is `profiles/default.json` |
| master file | the single coordinated IFC file for one placement area |
| level | one floor of a building: an `IfcBuildingStorey` |
| room | a named area with a floor, modelled as an `IfcSpace` (the IFC entity name; here it always means "room or zone") |
| zone | a named volume that is data only: an `IfcSpatialZone` |
| declaration property | a named property this set asks you to write because consumers read it (for example `RoomId`); a profile can rename them |
| extension | an optional group of rules a profile switches on when its consumer needs it: walkability, luminaires, signboards, furniture collision, terrain |

---

<!-- chunk: g1--2-what-the-profile-gives-you | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 2. What the profile gives you | rules: - -->
## 2. What the profile gives you

Before you start, get the profile of the consumer you build for. If you have none, use `profiles/default.json` and say so in
your delivery notes. If a number your work depends on is missing, ask the consumer; do not guess.

| Profile item | What it tells you | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| frame | which way +X and +Y point, the height of your local z = 0 in the consumer's frame, whether the file is placed as authored | `frame.horizontalAxes`, `frame.levelOffsetMetres`, `frame.placement` |
| limits and budgets | hard caps and recommended sizes | `limits.*`, `budgets.*` |
| identifiers | room identifier length and pattern, assigned entity-number range, allowed occupants | `identifiers.*`, `propertyNames` |
| geometry | doorway, stair and ramp values | `geometry.*` |
| volumes | the region to stay inside, regions to keep out, floors the consumer supplies | `buildVolume`, `keepOut`, `baseSurfaces` |
| extensions | whether it walks people through rooms, turns fixtures into lights, generates signs, simplifies furniture, supplies terrain | `extensions.*` |
| rule levels | rules it makes stricter or switches off | `ruleLevels` |

---

<!-- chunk: g1--3-file-and-schema | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 3. File and schema | rules: B-01,B-02,B-02a,B-03,B-04,B-05,B-06,B-07,B-08,B-09 -->
## 3. File and schema

**B-01 · REQUIRED** - Deliver an IFC schema edition the profile accepts (`schema.allowed`, default IFC4). Other editions may open in some tools, but files in an unlisted edition are not portable to that consumer.

**B-02 · REQUIRED** - Declare the length unit as metres (an `IfcSIUnit` `LENGTHUNIT` `METRE`, or a prefixed or conversion-based unit that resolves to metres) and model in it. A missing or misread unit rescales the whole building.

**B-02a · RECOMMENDED** - Prefer plain metres (a `METRE` unit with no prefix) over a prefixed or conversion-based unit, which some tools mishandle.

**B-03 · RECOMMENDED** - Deliver one coordinated master file per placement area, and send per-building files only as alternates. Several overlapping files for one area leave the consumer guessing which one is authoritative.

**B-04 · REQUIRED** - Keep the file plain ASCII: write every non-ASCII character with the format's escape (`\X2\00B7\X0\` for a middle dot, `\X2\2014\X0\` for a long dash). Raw bytes above 127 are read differently by different tools.

**B-05 · REQUIRED** - Stay within the profile's hard limits: `limits.maxFileMegabytes`, `limits.maxVertices` and `limits.maxTriangles`. A file over a consumer's cap is refused or truncated.

**B-06 · REQUIRED** - Use geometry that every common reader can display: swept solids (`IfcExtrudedAreaSolid` with rectangle, circle, arbitrary closed or arbitrary-with-voids profiles), faceted breps or polygonal face sets, and mapped items. Boolean-heavy breps, swept disks and unusual profiles are dropped by many readers without a message; `check_ifc.py` reports products that have a representation but yield no triangles.

**B-07 · RECOMMENDED** - Make the export deterministic: the same inputs give a byte-identical file (fixed timestamps, stable ordering, `GlobalId` values derived from stable keys). Consumers and reviewers compare revisions.

**B-08 · RECOMMENDED** - Write each STEP entity on a single line when the profile asks (`file.singleLineEntities`). Line-oriented tools, diff tools and simple readers handle such files; wrapped entities are valid but can be missed. A consumer that depends on it raises this rule to required.

**B-09 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep the file below the profile's recommended size, `budgets.recommendedFileMegabytes`. Large files load slowly and are hard to review.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--4-units-axes-origin-and-levels | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 4. Units, axes, origin and levels | rules: B-10,B-11,B-12,B-13,B-14,B-142,B-15 -->
## 4. Units, axes, origin and levels

**B-10 · REQUIRED** - Use a right-handed frame with Z up and the horizontal axes the profile states (`frame.horizontalAxes`), in metres. Models authored with another up axis come in turned over.

**B-11 · RECOMMENDED** - Author in the placement the profile expects (`frame.placement`): with `final`, local z = 0 is the finished floor of the lowest level and the consumer applies no offset or rotation, so author in the final placement frame. If you cannot, state the offset in the frame note (B-12).

**B-12 · RECOMMENDED** - State your frame in the file: a property set on the `IfcProject` with a text property `FrameNote` ("metres; +X forward; +Y left; +Z up; local z = 0 at the finished floor of the lowest level") and a number `LevelOffsetMetres`. A written note lets a reviewer or another tool verify the frame.

**B-13 · REQUIRED** - Create one `IfcBuildingStorey` for every level of every building, with a `Name` and a numeric `Elevation` equal to the level's finished-floor height in your file's frame, and make every element belong to one: contained (`IfcRelContainedInSpatialStructure`), aggregated (`IfcRelAggregates`) or, for zones, referenced (`IfcRelReferencedInSpatialStructure`). Elements without a level are dropped whenever a tool works level by level.

**B-14 · RECOMMENDED** - Use the full hierarchy `IfcProject` > `IfcSite` > `IfcBuilding` > `IfcBuildingStorey`, one `IfcBuilding` per building, and level names that start with the building name (`Clinic - ground / +0 m`).

**B-15 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep floor-to-floor heights regular so that stairs, lifts and openings line up between levels; make tall halls an exception you can name.

**B-142 · RECOMMENDED** - Put nothing below the lowest finished floor except slabs, footings, piles, walls, stairs, ramps, openings, the terrain element and reservation volumes. Foundations, retaining walls and a stair that goes down into the ground are ordinary on a slope; a door, window, room or piece of furniture below the lowest floor means the origin was put at the wrong height.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--5-rooms-and-zones | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 5. Rooms and zones | rules: B-143,B-20,B-21,B-22,B-23,B-24,B-25,B-26,B-27,B-28,B-29,B-30,B-31,B-32,B-33,B-34 -->
## 5. Rooms and zones

A room is the unit a consumer identifies, lists, lights, signs, and places people in.

**B-20 · REQUIRED** - Model every room as an `IfcSpace` (internal, `ELEMENT`) whose geometry is an upward extrusion of the room's floor outline: the lowest plane of the solid is the floor and the top is the underside of the ceiling or slab above. Tools derive the floor and area from that lowest plane, so the floor must be one flat horizontal plane.

**B-21 · REQUIRED** - Give every `IfcSpace` geometry. A room without geometry cannot be located, measured or shown.

**B-22 · REQUIRED** - Give every room that has a `RoomId` a value that is unique, and write it as an `IfcPropertySingleValue` inside an `IfcPropertySet` linked by `IfcRelDefinesByProperties`. Duplicate identifiers make every reference to a room ambiguous.

**B-23 · REQUIRED** - Make room identifiers meet the profile: at most `identifiers.roomIdMaxLength` characters and matching `identifiers.roomIdPattern`. Consumers print identifiers on labels and store them in fixed-width fields.

**B-24 · RECOMMENDED** - Give every room an `Occupant` (text): the organisation or use it belongs to. When the profile lists allowed values (`identifiers.occupants`) use one of them exactly; consumers classify rooms by this text.

**B-25 · RECOMMENDED** - Give every room a `Function` (text) describing its use. When the profile names a convention for circulation (`identifiers.circulationPrefix`), start corridors, lobbies, stair halls and streets with it.

**B-26 · RECOMMENDED** - Give every room a `RoomId`. Tools that find no identifier invent one from the room's name, and that changes when the name changes, which breaks every saved reference. A consumer that needs stable references raises this rule to required (`ruleLevels`).

**B-27 · RECOMMENDED** - Also supply, when known: `NetAreaSquareMetres` (number), `BaseLevelMetres` (number), `ClearHeightMetres` (number) and `Notes` (text). IFC's standard property set for rooms has related properties (for example `Reference` and `NetPlannedArea`); a profile may map the declaration names to those (`propertyNames`).

**B-28 · RECOMMENDED** - Give each room a complete, human-readable `Name`; names appear in lists and on labels.

**B-29 · RECOMMENDED** - Declare streets, paths, plazas and park areas as rooms too, with an identifier and a `Function`, so that they can be referred to, lit and signed. Open floor that belongs to no room has no identity.

**B-143 · RECOMMENDED** - Model an open-air room (terrace, courtyard, deck, path, plaza) as an `IfcSpace` with `PredefinedType` `EXTERNAL` and the boolean property `Enclosed` set to false, and an internal room with `Enclosed` true or absent. Its volume rises to what covers it, or to a nominal height where it is open to the sky. Consumers that look for enclosed rooms (lighting, walkability, ceilings) skip open-air rooms.

**B-30 · RECOMMENDED** - Let rooms on one level touch along wall centre lines but not overlap by more than the wall thickness; overlapping floors make "which room is this point in" ambiguous.

**B-31 · RECOMMENDED** - Draw the room outline at the inside wall faces so the floor area is the usable area.

**B-32 · RECOMMENDED** - Group rooms into buildings with a `BuildingId` property, and mark long-lived content separately from replaceable content with a `Layer` property (`permanent` or `interim`), so that a building can be swapped without touching its surroundings.

### What a consumer typically builds from a room

| Place field | Comes from |
|---|---|
| identifier | `RoomId` (or one invented from the name when missing) |
| name, function, occupant, notes | `Name`, `Function`, `Occupant`, `Notes` |
| kind and organisation | rules on `Function`, `Occupant`, `RoomId` and `Name` |
| level | the level that holds the room |
| floor and ceiling height | lowest and highest point of the room solid |
| area | floor triangles; `NetAreaSquareMetres` when given |
| centre, bounds, floor outline | the room solid and its floor |
| doors and neighbours | the openings filled by doors (B-41) |

### Walkability extension: standing points

These two rules apply when the profile enables `extensions.walkability` (a consumer that places people or agents in rooms).

**B-33 · REQUIRED · walkability** - Leave every enclosed room a floor area where a person can stand: at least `extensions.walkability.standingClearanceMetres` clear of furniture, equipment, rails and transport elements. A room whose whole floor is within that distance of fixed objects has no usable start point.

**B-34 · RECOMMENDED · walkability** - Keep a free floor circle of `extensions.walkability.freeCircleMetres` in every room, and leave clear aisles from seating to doors.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--6-walls-doors-windows-and-openings | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 6. Walls, doors, windows and openings | rules: B-40,B-40a,B-41,B-42,B-43,B-44,B-45,B-46,B-47,B-48 -->
## 6. Walls, doors, windows and openings

**B-40 · REQUIRED** - Model walls as `IfcWall` (`IfcWallStandardCase` is also read), not as generic proxies; consumers select, colour and count by class.

**B-40a · RECOMMENDED** - Use one element per maximal straight run rather than one per room edge.

**B-41 · REQUIRED** - Model every door as an `IfcDoor` that fills an `IfcOpeningElement` in the wall, linked with `IfcRelVoidsElement` (wall to opening) and `IfcRelFillsElement` (opening to door). Tools find doorways, count them and work out which rooms they connect from the opening; a door with no opening is a picture on a solid wall.

**B-42 · REQUIRED** - Keep every doorway passable: its clear height is at least `geometry.doorMinClearHeightMetres`, and nothing solid (a sill, a bar, a glazed panel, furniture) crosses the opening centre line at the heights in `geometry.doorwayProbeHeightsMetres`. A door leaf may stand open or closed in the model, but do not rely on it to block movement.

**B-43 · RECOMMENDED** - Make doorways at least `geometry.doorMinClearWidthMetres` wide.

**B-44 · REQUIRED** - Model every window as an `IfcWindow` in an `IfcOpeningElement` linked with the voids and fills relations, so the wall is cut where the window is.

**B-45 · RECOMMENDED** - Give glass a surface style with opacity below 1 (about 0.4 to 0.6), so that every consumer shows it as see-through.

**B-46 · RECOMMENDED** - Give walls their real thickness; zero-thickness walls and double walls confuse area, collision and rendering.

**B-47 · RECOMMENDED** - Make every room reachable through a doorway, an open edge or a stair from a circulation room.

**B-48 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not put a door in a floor or roof; floor apertures are slab openings (B-53).

---

<!-- chunk: g1--7-floors-roofs-ceilings-and-slab-openings | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 7. Floors, roofs, ceilings and slab openings | rules: B-144,B-50,B-51,B-51a,B-52,B-53,B-54,B-55 -->
## 7. Floors, roofs, ceilings and slab openings

**B-50 · RECOMMENDED** - Model every walkable floor, including walkable roofs, as an `IfcSlab` (`FLOOR` or `ROOF`) whose top face is the finished floor. Rooms standing on a floor the consumer supplies (`baseSurfaces`) need no slab of their own. Glass floors are slabs with a glass-like colour and opacity. A consumer that checks standing points or floor contact raises this to required.

**B-51 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not duplicate a floor the consumer already provides (`baseSurfaces`); two coplanar surfaces flicker.

**B-51a · RECOMMENDED** - Omit slabs that rest directly on a consumer-supplied floor, or make them very thin.

**B-52 · RECOMMENDED** - Give slabs a realistic thickness; very thin slabs are fine only for surface layers such as paving.

**B-53 · REQUIRED** - Cut every hole in a slab (stair wells, shafts, service drops) as an `IfcOpeningElement` linked by `IfcRelVoidsElement`, not as separate floor pieces that merely leave a gap.

**B-54 · RECOMMENDED** - Model ceilings or roofs. Many consumers draw no ceiling unless there is geometry; a room with nothing above it reads as open-topped. A ceiling is the underside of a slab or an `IfcCovering`.

**B-144 · RECOMMENDED** - Model a pitched or sloped roof with sloped `IfcSlab` `ROOF` pieces that follow the real pitch, and a wall whose faces lean (a battered wall) as one `IfcWall` with an inclined section, not as flat boxes or steps. Consumers that work out rain, snow, sight lines or shadows read the shape; a stepped approximation gives the wrong answer.

**B-55 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep your own structure clear of openings in surfaces the consumer supplies (`baseSurfaces`), with the margin the profile states.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--8-circulation-stairs-ramps-lifts-rails | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 8. Circulation, stairs, ramps, lifts, rails | rules: B-60,B-61,B-62,B-63,B-64,B-65,B-66,B-67 -->
## 8. Circulation, stairs, ramps, lifts, rails

**B-60 · REQUIRED** - Model each stair flight as an `IfcStairFlight` (a parent `IfcStair` without geometry is fine). Consumers recognise stairs, and simulators build their walking surface, from the flight.

**B-61 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep risers at or below `geometry.stairRiserLimitMetres`, with a landing and head-room; avoid winding and spiral stairs unless you have checked the consumer reads them.

**B-62 · RECOMMENDED** - Give every multi-level building at least one real stair. Lifts drawn in IFC are often static solids; a stair is the one way between levels that every consumer understands.

**B-63 · RECOMMENDED** - Draw lifts as `IfcTransportElement` with `PredefinedType` `ELEVATOR`, with properties such as `Service`, `StopsMetres` and `ShaftWidthMetres`.

**B-64 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep every walked slope at or below `geometry.rampMaxSlope` (rise over run) except stairs, and give ramps a clear width at least as wide as a doorway. Model ramps as `IfcRamp` with `IfcRampFlight`, or as a sloped `IfcSlab`.

**B-65 · RECOMMENDED · walkability** - Do not leave low obstacles up to `extensions.walkability.stepHeightMetres` high (floor boxes, square-edged wedges) that a walker steps over unseen; ramp them or make them visible steps.

**B-66 · RECOMMENDED** - Model rails (`IfcRailing`) with cheap geometry: simple posts and one rail section. Rails with dense tessellation are a common cause of heavy files.

**B-67 · RECOMMENDED · walkability** - Know which classes the consumer treats as not solid (`extensions.walkability.nonSolidClasses`) and model walk-through areas with those classes or with reservation volumes (B-80); everything else may block movement.

### Clearance and size summary

| Item | Value | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| doorway clear height | at least `geometry.doorMinClearHeightMetres` | B-42 |
| doorway probe heights | `geometry.doorwayProbeHeightsMetres` | B-42 |
| doorway clear width | at least `geometry.doorMinClearWidthMetres` | B-43 |
| stair riser | at most `geometry.stairRiserLimitMetres` | B-61 |
| walked ramp slope | at most `geometry.rampMaxSlope` | B-64 |
| free floor around fixed objects | `extensions.walkability.standingClearanceMetres` | B-33 |
| free floor circle in a room | `extensions.walkability.freeCircleMetres` | B-34 |

---

<!-- chunk: g1--9-names-identifiers-property-sets-and-classifica | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 9. Names, identifiers, property sets and classification | rules: B-70,B-71,B-72,B-73,B-74,B-75,B-76 -->
## 9. Names, identifiers, property sets and classification

**B-70 · REQUIRED** - Give every product a unique 22-character IFC `GlobalId` that does not change between exports. `GlobalId` is the key tools use to match an element across revisions and across files.

**B-71 · RECOMMENDED** - Number your IFC entities from the start the profile assigns (`identifiers.entityNumberStart`, when set) so that files from several authors can be merged without clashes.

**B-72 · RECOMMENDED** - Write declaration properties as text, number or boolean values in `IfcPropertySingleValue` entries of an `IfcPropertySet` linked by `IfcRelDefinesByProperties` on the product itself. Many readers ignore quantity sets, enumerations, tables and properties on types.

**B-73 · RECOMMENDED** - Use one descriptive property set per topic (`Pset_Declaration_Room`, ...) and put only declaration properties in it.

**B-74 · RECOMMENDED** - If your organisation uses a classification scheme, attach it with `IfcRelAssociatesClassification`. Many consumers ignore it, so never make it the only place a meaning is written.

**B-75 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep identifiers stable across revisions: an unchanged room, door or fixture keeps its `RoomId`, `GlobalId` and declaration ids. Replace an element by giving the new one a new id and retiring the old.

**B-76 · RECOMMENDED** - Give your own identifiers dotted prefixes (`arch.entrance`, `clinic.lobby`), at most 160 characters, no control characters.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--10-zones-and-reserved-volumes | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 10. Zones and reserved volumes | rules: B-80,B-81,B-81a,B-82 -->
## 10. Zones and reserved volumes

**B-80 · RECOMMENDED** - Declare a volume that must stay empty or must not be solid (a sight line, a clearance, a service corridor) twice: as an `IfcSpatialZone`, and (so it can be seen) as an `IfcBuildingElementProxy` with `PredefinedType` `PROVISIONFORSPACE`. That is the standard IFC way to mark a reserved provision: consumers that understand it leave the proxy out of physical models; any other proxy is a solid thing.

**B-81 · RECOMMENDED** - Give every zone a unique identifier (`ZoneId` or, if missing, its `Name`) and its own geometry; a zone without geometry cannot be shown or selected.

**B-81a · RECOMMENDED** - Always supply `ZoneId`, plus `ZoneClass` (for example `observation-sightline`) and `Requirement` (a sentence saying what must stay clear).

**B-82 · RECOMMENDED** - Use zones to record viewing intent (a downward sight line from a mezzanine); ordinary glass cannot be one-way, and who may look is a consumer decision, not a file property.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--11-optional-extension-lighting-fixtures | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 11. Optional extension: lighting fixtures | rules: B-90,B-91,B-92,B-92a,B-93,B-94,B-95 -->
## 11. Optional extension: lighting fixtures

These rules apply when the profile enables `extensions.luminaires` (a consumer that turns declared fixtures into lights). Property names are those of the profile (`propertyNames`).

**B-90 · REQUIRED · luminaires** - Model each fixture as an `IfcElementAssembly` that aggregates two `IfcLightFixture` parts: a housing, and an emissive part whose `Name` ends in the profile's suffix (`extensions.luminaires.lensNameSuffix`). The emissive part is the one that glows.

**B-91 · REQUIRED · luminaires** - Put every property in `extensions.luminaires.requiredProperties` on the assembly, make `LuminaireId` unique, and use a `LightType` from `extensions.luminaires.lightTypes`. A fixture missing a property cannot be turned into a light.

| Property | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LuminaireId` | text | unique identifier |
| `LuminaireMount` | text | `pendant`, `ceiling`, `post`, `wall`, free text |
| `LightType` | text | one of the profile's light types |
| `LightEnergy` | number | strength in the consumer's units |
| `LightRangeM` | number | reach in metres |
| `LightSpotDeg` | number | cone angle in degrees |
| `LightColor` | text `"r,g,b"` | each 0 to 1 |
| `LightPosition` | text `"x,y,z"` | where the light sits, in the consumer's global frame (B-92) |
| `LightAim` | text `"x,y,z"` | unit vector the light points along |
| `LightFadeBeginM`, `LightFadeLengthM` | number | where the light starts to fade, and how long the fade is |
| `LuminaireTarget` | text, optional | the `RoomId` the fixture serves |

**B-92 · REQUIRED · luminaires** - Write `LightPosition` in the consumer's global frame: the file-local point plus `frame.levelOffsetMetres` (same x and y, z plus the offset); the geometry stays file-local. The emissive part's centre plus the offset must be within `extensions.luminaires.positionToleranceMetres` of the declared point.

**B-92a · RECOMMENDED · luminaires** - Give the file-local position as well (`LightPositionLocal`) so a reviewer can check the offset was applied once.

**B-93 · REQUIRED · luminaires** - Make `LightAim` a unit vector (length 1 within 1e-6) in the consumer's frame.

**B-94 · RECOMMENDED · luminaires** - Give every enclosed room at least one fixture (set `LuminaireTarget`), between the floor and the ceiling, in warm colours, not pointed at glazing.

**B-95 · RECOMMENDED · luminaires** - Count the lights: every declared fixture may become a real light, and the consumer may cap them per room (`extensions.luminaires.maxPerRoom`).

---

<!-- chunk: g1--12-optional-extension-signboards | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 12. Optional extension: signboards | rules: B-100,B-101,B-102,B-103 -->
## 12. Optional extension: signboards

These rules apply when the profile enables `extensions.signboards` (a consumer that generates signs from declared boards).

**B-100 · REQUIRED · signboards** - Model a board as an `IfcElementAssembly` carrying every property in `extensions.signboards.requiredProperties`, with a `SignboardKind` from `extensions.signboards.kinds`.

| Property | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `SignboardId` | text | unique identifier |
| `SignboardKind` | text | one of the profile's kinds (default `entrance_board`, `stop_board`) |
| `SignboardText`, `SignboardSub` | text | main text, optional second line |
| `SignboardWidthM`, `SignboardHeightM` | number | board size in metres |
| `SignboardReadM` | number | distance in metres from which it must be readable |
| `SignboardPosition` | text `"x,y,z"` | centre, in the consumer's global frame (B-92) |
| `SignboardNormal` | text `"x,y,z"` | unit vector pointing away from the board's face |

**B-101 · REQUIRED · signboards** - Make the main text fit the board: allow about 0.55 times the capital height of width per character plus a margin of 12 % of the board height on each side; text that cannot be fitted at a capital height of 0.05 m is an error.

**B-102 · RECOMMENDED · signboards** - Declare a reading distance your letters support: capital height in metres must be at least `pixels * readM / extensions.signboards.displayPixelsPerRadian`, with pixels from `extensions.signboards.minCapitalPixels` (primary text), and the distance within `extensions.signboards.readingDistanceMetres`.

**B-103 · RECOMMENDED · signboards** - Declare an entrance board on the wall's outer face, not the wall centre plane, and keep lamps and trees away from its face.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--13-geometry-hygiene | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 13. Geometry hygiene | rules: B-110,B-111,B-112,B-113,B-114,B-115,B-116 -->
## 13. Geometry hygiene

**B-110 · REQUIRED** - Keep all geometry inside the profile's build volume (`buildVolume`) and outside its keep-out regions (`keepOut`), when it gives them; check every vertex, not only footprints. The terrain element of the terrain extension (section 16) is context supplied by the consumer's terrain source and is not checked against the build volume.

**B-111 · RECOMMENDED** - Make solids closed and consistently oriented: no missing faces, no inside-out solids, no zero-area or duplicate faces.

**B-112 · RECOMMENDED** - Avoid coplanar overlapping faces (two walls sharing a face, a covering lying exactly on a wall, a slab exactly on a floor). Offset thin layers or merge them.

**B-113 · RECOMMENDED** - Use mapped items (`IfcMappedItem` with `IfcRepresentationMap`) for repeated parts. They keep files small; most consumers expand them to ordinary triangles, so they save file size, not drawing cost.

**B-114 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not model what cannot be seen or used: hidden interiors, bolts, hinge detail, text as geometry, curves with more than `geometry.maxCurveSegmentsPerCircle` segments per full circle.

**B-115 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not model terrain, soil or relief in IFC unless the profile says how. Trees and planting may be `IfcGeographicElement` markers; consumers differ on whether they are solid. The terrain extension (section 16) is how a profile says how: with it, the only terrain in the file is the derived patch it describes.

**B-116 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not model a thin layer at a height where the consumer adds its own surface layer (floor finishes laid on the room floor); two layers at one height flicker.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--14-level-of-detail-and-budgets | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 14. Level of detail and budgets | rules: B-120,B-121 -->
## 14. Level of detail and budgets

Triangle count drives load time; the number of distinct materials and objects drives drawing cost. Hard caps are `limits.*` (B-05); recommended sizes are `budgets.*`.

| Quantity | Profile parameter | Default |
|---|---|---|
| file size, hard | `limits.maxFileMegabytes` | 250 MB |
| vertices, hard | `limits.maxVertices` | 10,000,000 |
| triangles, hard | `limits.maxTriangles` | 5,000,000 |
| file size, recommended | `budgets.recommendedFileMegabytes` | 100 MB |
| triangles, recommended | `budgets.recommendedTriangles` | 1,000,000 |
| distinct (class, colour, opacity) combinations | `budgets.maxDistinctColours` | 50 |

**B-120 · RECOMMENDED** - Stay under the profile's recommended triangle count, `budgets.recommendedTriangles`. A constrained consumer publishes a much lower figure; build to the profile you were given. Terrain triangles are counted separately (B-138).

**B-121 · RECOMMENDED** - Spend triangles where the viewer looks: entrances, interiors a person stands in, anything within arm's reach. Distant detail is wasted.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--15-what-to-avoid | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 15. What to avoid | rules: - -->
## 15. What to avoid

* A floor that duplicates one the consumer supplies (B-51).
* Doors without openings, or openings without doors (B-41).
* Anything across a doorway (B-42).
* Rooms without identifiers or with duplicates (B-22, B-26).
* Heavily tessellated rails and balusters (B-66).
* Low steps and ledges nobody can see (B-65, with the walkability extension).
* A proxy used for something that must be walk-through; use a reservation volume (B-80).
* Missing ceilings (B-54).
* Elements outside any level (B-13).
* Geometry readers drop silently (B-06).
* One-way glass promises: ordinary glass is two-way.
* Changing identifiers between revisions (B-75).
* Cutting a pad, a cut or a fill into the terrain element, or modelling water in the file (B-130, B-139).

---

<!-- chunk: g1--16-optional-extension-terrain-context | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 16. Optional extension: terrain context | rules: - -->
## 16. Optional extension: terrain context

Some consumers place a building in a world whose ground comes from their own terrain source. There the terrain stays authoritative in
the source. In IFC it is **derived, read-only context**: a terrain element built from a patch the source gives you, used for
placement, clash and "is the building floating or buried" checks. The extension applies when `extensions.terrain.enabled` is true;
its numbers are in `extensions.terrain.*`.

The work flows like this:

1. **Send** the source three things: the footprint polygon of every ground-contact level, the finished floor elevation of each (height above
   sea level of its finished floor) and a grading rule (`extensions.terrain.grading`, for example cut and fill slopes no steeper than 1:2). `tools/site_request.py` writes them from the master file.
2. **Receive** a height patch: a GeoTIFF with one float32 band in metres, cut round the building with a margin, at one source level
   (one pixel size), and a JSON sidecar (`schemas/terrain-patch.schema.json`) with the source package version and hash, origin, pixel size, CRS
   definition, vertical datum and licence. The source grades the pad and clears vegetation inside the footprint plus a margin
   (`extensions.terrain.clearingMarginMetres`). Its baseline ground is natural, with no built features; the building is an overlay
   layer and never part of the terrain.
3. **Import** with `tools/terrain_import.py`: it reduces the samples to a triangulated network within a stated error bound, converts
   to the file frame and writes the elements the rules below describe.
4. **Check** with `check_ifc.py` and a profile that enables the extension.

Say which frame each number is in:

| Where | Frame |
|---|---|
| sidecar and site request | site frame: x east, y north, z up, metres, centred on the site; heights above mean sea level, with sea level exactly 0 |
| IFC file | file frame: the site frame shifted by the building origin and turned by the building azimuth (the angle from east, counter-clockwise, to the file's +X axis), z measured from the lowest finished floor |
| the consumer's own runtime | whatever it uses (for example x east, y up, z south); the consumer converts, you never write it |

The site frame is a custom azimuthal frame on a sphere, not a registry code. `IfcProjectedCRS.Name` carries the profile's name for it
(`extensions.terrain.crsName`) and `Description` carries the definition from the sidecar.

---

<!-- chunk: g1--17-terrain-context-the-rules | source: 01-builders-and-architects-guide.md | title: 17. Terrain context: the rules | rules: B-130,B-131,B-132,B-133,B-134,B-135,B-136,B-137,B-138,B-139,B-140,B-141 -->
## 17. Terrain context: the rules

These rules apply when `extensions.terrain.enabled` is true (section 16 explains the flow and the frames).

**B-130 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Deliver the terrain as exactly one `IfcGeographicElement` with `PredefinedType` `TERRAIN`, contained in the `IfcSite`, whose body is one `IfcTriangulatedFaceSet`. It is derived, read-only context: do not edit its heights, and do not cut pads, cuts, fills or building features into it. The terrain source does grading and clearing before it cuts the patch, so the world and the model agree.

**B-131 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Make the terrain a valid heightfield over a rectangular patch: every triangle faces up and has area, no edge belongs to more than two triangles, and the triangles cover the patch rectangle exactly once. Consumers sample the surface by plan position, so an overhang, a hole or an overlap gives two heights or none for one point.

**B-132 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Make the terrain cover the building: the plan points of the slabs and walls of every ground-contact level, grown by `extensions.terrain.footprintMarginMetres`, lie inside the patch. A patch that stops short of the footprint cannot answer where the ground is under the building.

**B-133 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Georeference the file with an `IfcMapConversion` from the model context to an `IfcProjectedCRS` named `extensions.terrain.crsName`, in metres, with the local X axis set to the building azimuth (a unit vector, east when the building is not turned), scale 1 and `OrthogonalHeight` equal to the height above sea level of the lowest finished floor (local z = 0). The name need not be a registry code. The profile's `frame.levelOffsetMetres` must be 0, because the floor height is carried here and not by an offset.

**B-134 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Set `IfcSite.RefElevation` to the terrain height at the building origin above sea level, within `extensions.terrain.siteElevationToleranceMetres` of the terrain element at that point. The site elevation and the terrain must tell one story about where the ground is.

**B-135 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Do not put a building in water: the terrain at every footprint point of every ground-contact level is at or above `extensions.terrain.seaLevelMetres`, and `FootprintInWater` is not true. Terrain below sea level is seabed.

**B-136 · RECOMMENDED · terrain** - Do not let the building float or sink: no ground-contact level's floor is above the terrain by more than `extensions.terrain.floatToleranceMetres` at every footprint point of that level, or below it by more than `extensions.terrain.buryToleranceMetres` at every one. A house on a slope may stand above the ground at one edge and below it at another; that is allowed. A building above or below the ground everywhere was placed at the wrong height. The check is an estimate from the footprint points, so it starts as a warning; a consumer that relies on it raises it in `ruleLevels`.

**B-137 · REQUIRED · terrain** - Pin the terrain source in a property set `Pset_Declaration_Terrain` on the terrain element: `Role` (`derived-context`), `PackageName`, `PackageVersion`, `PackageSha256`, `PatchSha256`, `PatchLevel`, `PixelSizeMetres`, `ErrorBoundMetres` (at most `extensions.terrain.maxErrorBoundMetres`), `Frame` and `VerticalDatum`. Heights near water can change between source versions, so a delivery says exactly which version it was built on and never carries numbers from an earlier one.

**B-138 · RECOMMENDED · terrain** - Keep the terrain within `extensions.terrain.maxTriangles`. Terrain triangles do not count against `budgets.recommendedTriangles`; they still count against the hard limits of B-05.

**B-139 · RECOMMENDED · terrain** - Keep water out of the file and declare it as metadata in `Pset_Declaration_Site` on the `IfcSite`: `SeaLevelMetres`, `FootprintInWater` and, when known, `DistanceToShoreMetres`. Sea and shoreline belong to the terrain source; the file only says how the building relates to them.

**B-140 · RECOMMENDED · terrain** - State the frame of the terrain numbers: `Pset_Declaration_Terrain.Frame` says that the file frame is x east, y north, z up and relative to the lowest finished floor. Never write coordinates in a consumer's runtime frame.

**B-141 · RECOMMENDED · terrain** - Declare every level that touches the ground with `GroundContact` true in `Pset_Declaration_Level`; without a declaration the lowest level is the only ground-contact level. On a stepped or terraced site several levels meet the ground, each at its own height, and the terrain source needs each footprint and floor elevation to grade them. The checker warns about an undeclared level that sits on the terrain.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--introduction | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# Guide 2: Interior Decorator's Guide

For interior decorators, material authors and texture artists who define finishes, wall coverings, floor and ceiling
treatments, accents and trims, and who deliver a reusable material library.

Rule levels and the profile mechanism are explained in the [README](README.md); profile parameters appear in `backticks`
(full list: [07-profile-parameters.md](07-profile-parameters.md)). Read sections 1 to 4 of guide 1 first: finishes attach to
the rooms and element classes defined there.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--1-how-consumers-decide-what-a-surface-looks-like | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 1. How consumers decide what a surface looks like | rules: - -->
## 1. How consumers decide what a surface looks like

Consumers differ here, which is why this guide is built around a portable method.

1. **IFC carries a colour and an opacity per surface style.** `IfcSurfaceStyle` with a rendering colour and a transparency is
   read by every common reader. Texture images, texture coordinates and physically based settings are read by some and ignored by
   many, so a file that relies on them looks different (or flat) in other tools.
2. **A finish schedule says what each style means.** You deliver a small JSON file that maps every (element class, colour,
   opacity) key used in the IFC to a finish: which texture set, how large one tile is, how strongly to tint it. A consumer that
   has its own materials can follow the schedule; one that does not still shows your colours.
3. **Texture sets are delivered separately,** as folders of images with a description file, so that any consumer can load them
   with its own mapping (projection, UVs, atlases).
4. **Floors, ceilings and walls use faces.** A finish can describe up to three face slots: `top` (faces pointing up, the walking
   surface), `side` (edges) and `bottom` (faces pointing down, which is the ceiling of the room below); most classes use `all`.
5. **Only emissive parts glow.** In consumers that turn fixtures into lights, the glow comes from the fixture part the profile
   names (guide 1, section 11), not from a colour.

What you control is: the class of each element, the colour and opacity you give it, the finish schedule, and the texture sets.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--2-colour-rules | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 2. Colour rules | rules: D-01,D-02,D-03,D-04,D-05,D-06,D-07,D-08 -->
## 2. Colour rules

**D-01 · REQUIRED** - Give each distinct finish its own colour within an element class. The schedule keys finishes by (class, colour, opacity); two finishes with the same key are one finish. Colours that differ by less than 1/255 in every channel are the same colour.

**D-02 · REQUIRED** - Give the same finish the same colour and opacity on every element that uses it. A small drift (from re-rounding in another tool) creates a new key that has no schedule entry.

**D-03 · REQUIRED** - When you deliver a finish schedule, include an entry for every (class, colour, opacity) combination that appears in your IFC files. The checker lists them (`finishKeys`).

**D-04 · RECOMMENDED** - Use opacity below 1 only for glass and other see-through things (about 0.4 to 0.6 for glazing). Consumers treat anything with an opacity below 1 as see-through. A walkable glass floor is a slab with a glass colour and opacity.

**D-05 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep the palette small: at most `budgets.maxDistinctColours` combinations (default 50). Every combination is one more material to map, load and draw.

**D-06 · RECOMMENDED** - Treat the IFC colour as a design tint: the schedule says how strongly it is blended into the texture (0 means the texture alone, 1 the colour fully). Pick a colour near the intended look, not a code colour such as pure red.

**D-07 · RECOMMENDED** - Avoid pure black, pure white and very dark large surfaces: they clip or disappear under typical lighting. Keep large floors and walls between about 0.25 and 0.85 in mean linear luminance unless a dark look is the point.

**D-08 · RECOMMENDED** - Choose neutral tints for fabrics; strongly coloured tints shift under lighting.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--3-floors-ceilings-wall-coverings-accents-and-tri | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 3. Floors, ceilings, wall coverings, accents and trims | rules: D-10,D-11,D-12,D-13,D-20,D-21,D-30,D-31,D-32,D-33,D-34,D-35 -->
## 3. Floors, ceilings, wall coverings, accents and trims

### Floors

**D-10 · RECOMMENDED** - When you deliver a finish schedule, give every room that has a floor a floor finish: list them in the `floors` section by `Occupant`, by `RoomId` list or by pattern, plus a default. A room without a rule gets whatever the consumer defaults to.

**D-11 · RECOMMENDED** - Also write a text property `Finish` on each room (for example `light warm-grey resilient floor; pale ivory walls`), so that the intent stays with the room.

**D-12 · RECOMMENDED** - Change floor finishes at door lines, not mid-room, and keep a visible threshold between unlike finishes.

**D-13 · RECOMMENDED** - Choose low-gloss, light floors for rooms people work in: dark glossy floors read as black under many lighting set-ups.

### Ceilings

**D-20 · RECOMMENDED** - Decide ceilings through the slab or roof above: the `bottom` face of the slab above is the ceiling of the room below. To get a different ceiling finish give that slab a different colour, and describe its `bottom` slot in the schedule. A ceiling can also be an `IfcCovering` (D-31).

**D-21 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep ceiling finishes matte and light; glossy ceilings amplify lamp hot spots.

### Wall coverings

**D-30 · RECOMMENDED** - Express a wall finish through the wall element's own colour (one colour per finish and per class). It works in every consumer.

**D-31 · RECOMMENDED** - Use an `IfcCovering` (`PredefinedType` `CLADDING`, `FLOORING`, `CEILING` or `WRAPPING`) only when a finish covers part of a wall, or a surface that has no element of its own. Model it as a shell at least 10 mm thick whose back face sits exactly on the surface (touching, not overlapping), so no two faces share a plane and face the same way. Support for `IfcCovering` varies between consumers, so confirm it with the consumer first.

**D-32 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not rely on a texture pattern starting at an edge: consumers project textures differently. Design coverings that tolerate any start position, or model panels as geometry when joints must line up.

### Accents and trims

**D-33 · RECOMMENDED** - Make skirtings, cornices, door frames, handrails and accent bands separate elements with their own colour, at least 1 cm thick. Elements thinner than about 5 mm flicker against what they sit on.

**D-34 · RECOMMENDED** - Accent features (a feature wall, a coloured door, a timber panel) are a colour on the element in the same class as its neighbours, not an image inside the IFC.

### Glass

**D-35 · RECOMMENDED** - Describe glass by colour, opacity and three optional settings: base opacity, edge reflection (`fresnelAlpha`) and smudge roughness (`smudgeRough`). Keep glass light and clear: dark or green glass reads as black or milky in many viewers.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--4-texture-sets | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 4. Texture sets | rules: D-40,D-41,D-42,D-43,D-44,D-45,D-46,D-47,D-48,D-49,D-50 -->
## 4. Texture sets

A texture set is a folder of images plus a description; it is the unit of a material library.

**D-40 · REQUIRED** - Deliver every texture set as a folder `<setName>/` containing the maps the profile lists (`textures.maps`, default `albedo.png`, `normal.png`, `orm.png`) and `set.json`.

**D-41 · REQUIRED** - Use these encodings, so that every consumer reads the maps the same way:

| Map | Content | Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| `albedo.png` | base colour | 8-bit RGB PNG, **sRGB** encoded, no alpha, no baked lighting or shadows |
| `normal.png` | surface relief | 8-bit RGB PNG, **linear** data, tangent basis, flat surface = (128, 128, 255); green channel direction as the profile states (`textures.normalConvention`: `+Y` up, or `-Y`) |
| `orm.png` | packed material data | 8-bit RGB PNG, **linear** data. **R** = ambient occlusion (255 = unoccluded), **G** = roughness (0 = mirror, 255 = fully rough), **B** = metalness |

**D-42 · RECOMMENDED** - Make the texture tile seamlessly in both directions; consumers repeat it across large surfaces, and a seam repeats with it. Check the three-by-three preview.

**D-43 · REQUIRED** - Declare the physical size of one tile in `set.json` as `tileMetres`, so that a consumer can scale it correctly.

**D-44 · RECOMMENDED** - Use square, power-of-two images, all maps the same size, one of `textures.sizesPixels` (default 512, 1024, 2048). Larger maps cost memory in every view.

**D-45 · RECOMMENDED** - Choose the tile size so the texel density is inside `textures.densityPixelsPerMetre` (default 250 to 2500 pixels per metre): for 1024 pixels that is a tile of about 0.4 m to 4 m.

**D-46 · RECOMMENDED** - Avoid fine, regular weaves and stripes with a tile under 0.5 m: they produce moire at grazing angles.

**D-47 · RECOMMENDED** - Declare `tintMode` in `set.json` (one of `textures.tintModes`): `multiply` when the albedo is a near-neutral light map meant to be tinted by the IFC colour, or `authored` when the colour in the map is final.

**D-48 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep the pattern free of one-off features (a single stain, one knot) that would repeat visibly, and do not bake low-frequency variation in; consumers can add it.

**D-49 · RECOMMENDED** - If a pattern has a direction (planks, brushed metal, grain), say which image axis it follows in `set.json` (`direction`: `u`, `v` or `none`); consumers decide how directional patterns are oriented on floors and walls.

**D-50 · RECOMMENDED** - Check your tiles in a three-by-three arrangement and at a long viewing distance: fine relief that reads as speckle should be softened.

### set.json

```json
{
  "name": "plaster_fine",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "sizePixels": 1024,
  "tileMetres": 2.0,
  "tintMode": "multiply",
  "direction": "none",
  "normalConvention": "+Y",
  "description": "fine trowelled plaster, low sheen",
  "maps": { "albedo": "albedo.png", "normal": "normal.png", "orm": "orm.png" },
  "generator": "optional: script and seed that reproduce the set"
}
```

---

<!-- chunk: g2--5-the-finish-schedule | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 5. The finish schedule | rules: D-60,D-61,D-62,D-63 -->
## 5. The finish schedule

The finish schedule tells a consumer what each colour and each room floor means. The machine-readable shape is
`schemas/finish-schedule.schema.json`; a starting file is `templates/finish-schedule.template.json`.

**D-60 · REQUIRED** - Deliver `finish-schedule.json` with these sections: `format` (`finish-schedule/1`), `delivery`, `version` (SemVer), `materials[]` (one entry per (class, colour, opacity) key: `key`, `role`, `usedBy`, `faces`), `floors[]` (ordered floor rules: `where` and `finish`), and `libraries[]` (the texture-set folders it names, with versions).

**D-61 · REQUIRED** - Name only texture sets that exist: each face entry names a set from your delivery or from a library the profile or consumer publishes. Settings are optional:

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `set` | texture-set name |
| `tint` | `"ifc"` (the element's colour), a colour such as `"#5a5654"`, or `"none"` |
| `tintStrength` | 0 to 1: how far the tint replaces the texture's own colour |
| `tileMetres` | override the set's tile size |
| `normalScale` | strength of relief (typically 0.4 to 1.3) |
| `roughMul`, `metalMul` | multipliers on roughness and metalness |
| `macroStrength`, `macroScaleMetres` | optional low-frequency variation to hide repetition |
| `aoStrength` | strength of baked occlusion |
| `sheen`, `sheenTint` | fabric edge response |
| `offsetMetres` | shift the pattern so neighbouring materials do not repeat in step |

**D-62 · RECOMMENDED** - Mark materials that must stay as they are (emissive strips, planning markers) with `"keep": true` and a reason instead of giving them a texture.

**D-63 · RECOMMENDED** - Treat the schedule as a proposal: a consumer applies what it can. Do not depend on any single setting being honoured exactly.

### A short example

```json
{
  "format": "finish-schedule/1",
  "delivery": "example-room-1.0.0",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "materials": [
    { "key": { "class": "IfcWall", "colour": "#d9d2c3", "opacity": 1.0 },
      "role": "room walls", "usedBy": "all rooms",
      "faces": { "all": { "set": "plaster_fine", "tint": "ifc", "tintStrength": 0.55, "normalScale": 0.6 } } },
    { "key": { "class": "IfcSlab", "colour": "#c9c4b8", "opacity": 1.0 },
      "role": "floor slab", "usedBy": "all levels",
      "faces": { "top": { "set": "concrete_polished", "tint": "ifc", "tintStrength": 0.25 },
                 "side": { "set": "board_concrete" },
                 "bottom": { "set": "ceiling_gypsum" } } }
  ],
  "floors": [
    { "id": "floor-default", "where": { "occupant": "*" }, "finish": { "set": "oak_plank_wide" } }
  ],
  "libraries": [ { "name": "plaster_fine", "version": "1.0.0" } ]
}
```

---

<!-- chunk: g2--6-palettes | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 6. Palettes | rules: D-70,D-71,D-72 -->
## 6. Palettes

**D-70 · RECOMMENDED** - Build the palette from a few families and give each organisation or zone a distinct tint rather than a distinct pattern.

**D-71 · RECOMMENDED** - Describe the intent in words as well as colours ("light warm-grey resilient floor; pale ivory washable walls; low gloss"), so that a consumer with its own material library can choose.

**D-72 · RECOMMENDED** - Do not use texture or colour to carry meaning that labels already carry (room names, identifiers, directions). Use finish to make places feel different, not to label them.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--7-delivering-a-reusable-material-library | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 7. Delivering a reusable material library | rules: D-80,D-81,D-82,D-83,D-84,D-85 -->
## 7. Delivering a reusable material library

A library is a set of texture sets plus a finish schedule, with a manifest (guide 4). It is reusable when a different building can name your sets in its own schedule. `finishes/library.json` (`schemas/material-library.schema.json`) lists the sets and the schedule.

**D-80 · REQUIRED** - Record the source and licence of every texture set and every image in it in a `SOURCES.csv` next to the library with the columns `asset,type,source,licence,notes`. State whether the set is procedural (and which script and seed make it) or derived from photographs (and whose). Include no image whose licence you cannot state.

**D-81 · REQUIRED** - Include the SHA-256 hash of every file in the manifest (guide 4).

**D-82 · RECOMMENDED** - Prefer procedural sets with the generator and its seeds included; byte-identical output lets a consumer verify and regenerate the library and keeps the delivery small.

**D-83 · RECOMMENDED** - Name sets in lower case with underscores (`limewash_mottled`) and finishes with dotted names (`wall.limewash.warm`). Give each set its own SemVer; a changed look is a new version, never an overwrite.

**D-84 · RECOMMENDED** - Include a contact sheet (a PNG with each set's albedo, normal and roughness side by side, plus the tile size) so a reviewer sees the library at a glance.

**D-85 · RECOMMENDED** - Keep the library independent of any one building: no file name, label or set name should refer to a particular project.

---

<!-- chunk: g2--8-defects-commonly-seen | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: 8. Defects commonly seen | rules: - -->
## 8. Defects commonly seen

| Defect | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| fabrics read pale or tinted | strongly coloured tint | neutral tint, lower sheen (D-08) |
| stone chips too bold | high chip contrast | soften relief and chip mask |
| woven wall cloth shows moire | small tile, strong relief | larger tile, lower relief (D-46) |
| carpets and floors read near black | very low albedo | lighter albedo (D-07) |
| parquet reads as staggered strips | pattern repeat scale | check the three-by-three view (D-50) |
| concrete pores read as spots | relief too sharp | soften relief (D-50) |
| glazing milky or black | dark or green glass colour | light clear glass (D-35) |
| blotchy walls | uneven lighting plus strong variation | moderate variation (D-48) |

---

<!-- chunk: g2--exported-appearance-review | source: 02-interior-decorators-guide.md | title: Exported appearance review | rules: - -->
## Exported appearance review

Review UV scale, grain direction, masonry corners, normal strength, surface-specific roughness/metallic response and clear-glass optics in the actual exported consumer artifact. An exporter or preview must not silently replace authored surfaces to make its image look correct. Inspect closeups and ordinary room views; use [guide 9](09-environment-review-and-handoff.md) to record evidence and limitations.

---

<!-- chunk: g3--introduction | source: 03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# Guide 3: Furniture and Fixtures Guide

For designers who deliver furniture, equipment, fixtures and accents as reusable items that can be placed in any compatible
consumer.

Rule levels and the profile mechanism are explained in the [README](README.md); profile parameters appear in `backticks`
(full list: [07-profile-parameters.md](07-profile-parameters.md)). Read sections 1 to 4 and 14 of guide 1 first, and section 1
of guide 2.

---

<!-- chunk: g3--1-what-consumers-do-with-an-item | source: 03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md | title: 1. What consumers do with an item | rules: - -->
## 1. What consumers do with an item

An item reaches a consumer as an element inside a building's master IFC file. What happens next differs, but these things are common:

| Stage | What typically happens | Consequence for you |
|---|---|---|
| Reading | the class of the element and its geometry are read; declaration properties are read by name | use the right class (section 2) |
| Material | class, colour and opacity select a finish (guide 2) | distinct finish, distinct colour |
| Collision | furniture is approximated by a simple shape, often **one axis-aligned box** around the element, while fixed equipment may collide as exact triangles | a chair can be a solid block; do not rely on walking under a table. The profile states the mode (`extensions.furnitureCollision`) |
| Standing points | simulators keep a start point clear of furniture by a margin | leave free floor (guide 1, B-33, with the walkability extension) |
| Interaction | most consumers have no sit points, drawers or moving parts for IFC items | item data beyond the model is for placement tools |

An **item library** is a folder of single-item IFC files plus a description file per item. A building author places items into
the master file as instances (section 8).

---

<!-- chunk: g3--2-classes-and-categories | source: 03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md | title: 2. Classes and categories | rules: F-01,F-02,F-03 -->
## 2. Classes and categories

**F-01 · REQUIRED** - Use these classes for items, because consumers and tools are written for them, and make the description's class agree with the model.

| Item kind | IFC class | Typical consumer treatment |
|---|---|---|
| movable furniture (tables, chairs, benches, beds, shelves, sofas) | `IfcFurnishingElement` | simple shape or box; the default choice |
| fixed equipment, built-in units, counters, anything where the exact solid shape matters | `IfcBuildingElementProxy` (`PredefinedType` `USERDEFINED`, `ObjectType` set) | exact triangle mesh |
| light fixtures | `IfcElementAssembly` of two `IfcLightFixture` parts | see guide 1, section 11 |
| signs and boards | `IfcElementAssembly` | see guide 1, section 12 |
| rails and guards | `IfcRailing` | cheap geometry (guide 1, B-66) |
| lifts | `IfcTransportElement` (`ELEVATOR`) | usually static (guide 1, B-63) |

Other classes are drawn but get no special treatment; ask before using them for items.

**F-02 · RECOMMENDED** - Set `ObjectType` to a category word from this list so that reports and schedules can group items: `table`, `desk`, `seat`, `bench`, `sofa`, `bed`, `shelf`, `cabinet`, `counter`, `partition`, `planter`, `equipment`, `appliance`, `lamp`, `sign`, `accent`, `other`.

**F-03 · RECOMMENDED** - Add a property set `Pset_Declaration_Item` with text properties `ItemId` (the library id, section 3), `ItemVersion` (SemVer), `Role` (what the item is for, for example `work table`), and optionally `Occupant` and `PlanningStatus`.

---

<!-- chunk: g3--3-item-library-format | source: 03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md | title: 3. Item library format | rules: F-10,F-11,F-12 -->
## 3. Item library format

One item is one folder.

```
library/
  library.manifest.json          the package manifest (guide 4)
  items/
    table.work.1600/
      table.work.1600.ifc        one IfcFurnishingElement at the origin
      table.work.1600.item.json  the description (section 3.1)
      preview.png                optional, 512 by 512
  finishes/                      optional: finish schedule and texture sets (guide 2)
```

**F-10 · RECOMMENDED** - Make each item file IFC4 (guide 1, B-01 to B-06) containing exactly one furniture or equipment element, placed at the origin with no rotation, in metres, with a stable `GlobalId`. The item file needs a project, the length unit and a geometric context, but no building, levels or rooms.

**F-11 · RECOMMENDED** - Give every item a library id of the form `category.name.size` in lower case (for example `seat.stool.450`), unique within the library and never reused for a different design. The folder, the files, `ItemId` and the description all use the same id.

**F-12 · RECOMMENDED** - Provide a description file `<ItemId>.item.json` for every item (section 3.1). The checker and reviewers use it; schema: `schemas/item.schema.json`.

### 3.1 The description file

```json
{
  "format": "item/1",
  "itemId": "table.work.1600",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "name": "Work table, 1.6 m",
  "category": "table",
  "class": "IfcFurnishingElement",
  "pivot": { "kind": "floor", "description": "centre of the footprint, on the floor" },
  "front": [1, 0, 0],
  "dimensions": { "x": 1.6, "y": 0.8, "z": 0.74 },
  "footprint": [[-0.8, -0.4], [0.8, -0.4], [0.8, 0.4], [-0.8, 0.4]],
  "collision": { "kind": "box", "min": [-0.8, -0.4, 0.0], "max": [0.8, 0.4, 0.74] },
  "clearance": { "front": 0.9, "back": 0.0, "left": 0.45, "right": 0.45, "top": 0.0 },
  "anchors": [
    { "id": "seat-1", "kind": "seat", "position": [0.0, -0.7, 0.45], "direction": [0, 1, 0] },
    { "id": "work-surface", "kind": "surface", "position": [0.0, 0.0, 0.74], "direction": [0, 0, 1] }
  ],
  "placement": {
    "mounting": "floor",
    "againstWall": false,
    "rotations": [0, 90, 180, 270],
    "roomUses": ["work", "meeting", "study"],
    "avoid": ["circulation"],
    "minWallDistance": 0.0
  },
  "variants": [
    { "id": "oak", "colour": "#ccbba0", "finish": "furniture.oak.veneer" }
  ],
  "budget": { "triangles": 12, "textures": 0 },
  "provenance": { "author": "organisation name", "licence": "stated licence", "source": "original" }
}
```

---

<!-- chunk: g3--4-dimensions-origin-and-pivot | source: 03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md | title: 4. Dimensions, origin and pivot | rules: F-20,F-20a,F-21,F-22,F-23 -->
## 4. Dimensions, origin and pivot

**F-20 · REQUIRED** - Model in metres in the right-handed frame of guide 1 (B-02, B-10), with the item's own origin at its pivot (F-21).

**F-20a · RECOMMENDED** - Do not scale an item with an `IfcCartesianTransformationOperator` or any non-unit transform. Model it at its real size so that what you measure is what is drawn.

**F-21 · RECOMMENDED** - Put the pivot where the item meets the building, so placing it needs one point and one turn.

| Mounting | Pivot (origin) | Local axes |
|---|---|---|
| `floor` | centre of the footprint, on the floor (lowest point at z = 0) | +X is the front (the side a user faces and the side that needs clear floor), +Z up |
| `wall` | centre of the back face, at the mounting height in `placement.mountHeight` | +X is the front, pointing away from the wall |
| `ceiling` | centre of the fixing plane (the top of the item) | +Z stays up; the item hangs below the origin, so its dimensions run to negative z |
| `surface` | centre of the contact area on the thing it stands on | +X is the front |

**F-22 · RECOMMENDED** - Declare the bounding dimensions in the description and keep them equal (within 1 cm) to the measured size of the geometry.

**F-23 · RECOMMENDED** - Use true-to-life sizes: a work table is about 1.6 by 0.8 by 0.74 m, a chair about 0.5 by 0.55 by 0.85 m. Consumers do not scale items.

---

<!-- chunk: g3--5-placement-points-anchors-and-where-an-item-may | source: 03-furniture-and-fixtures-guide.md | title: 5. Placement points, anchors and where an item may be placed | rules: F-30,F-31,F-32,F-33,F-34 -->
## 5. Placement points, anchors and where an item may be placed

Most consumers ignore this data; it lets a placement tool, or a different consumer, place items without a person.

**F-30 · RECOMMENDED** - Declare anchors in item coordinates (metres, relative to the pivot). Anchor `kind` values: `seat` (where a person sits; direction = the way they face), `surface` (a usable top), `reach` (where a person stands to use it), `storage`, `power`, `door-swing` (a volume to keep clear), `mount` (where it attaches). Give each anchor an `id` unique within the item.
