---

<!-- chunk: params--rule-levels-in-a-profile | source: 07-profile-parameters.md | title: Rule levels in a profile | rules: - -->
## Rule levels in a profile

`ruleLevels` maps a rule id to `required`, `recommended` or `off`. The strict example makes these rules required: B-08, B-24, B-25, B-26, B-50, B-62, B-71.

---

<!-- chunk: params--extensions | source: 07-profile-parameters.md | title: Extensions | rules: - -->
## Extensions

An extension is an optional group of rules. It applies only when `extensions.<name>.enabled` is true: `walkability` (for consumers that place people or agents in rooms), `luminaires` (fixtures become lights), `signboards` (signs are generated from declared boards), `furnitureCollision` (furniture is approximated by a simple collider), `terrain` (the consumer's terrain source supplies the ground; the file carries a derived, read-only terrain patch). Rules that belong to an extension carry its name after the level, for example `B-90 REQUIRED luminaires`, and `rules.json` lists it in `extension`.

---

<!-- chunk: sub--introduction | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# How submissions and ingest work

This repository holds the guide set and it is also where outside contributors offer **deliveries**: buildings, interiors, furniture,
materials, fixtures and hardware. A delivery is reviewed as a pull request. When the maintainers merge it, a separate tool turns the
accepted delivery into separate, content-addressed component assets and a neutral catalogue. This page is for people and for software
agents; the rules the automatic checks enforce are X-70 to X-86 in guide 4, section 8 (X-79 to X-86 are the proofs, below).

---

<!-- chunk: sub--the-path-of-a-delivery | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: The path of a delivery | rules: - -->
## The path of a delivery

1. **Fork** this repository (your own copy on the hosting service).
2. **Build** the delivery in a branch of your fork, in the folder `deliveries/<slug>/`. The slug is lower-case letters, digits and single
   hyphens, for example `oak-study`. Follow guides 1 to 4 and the worked example (guide 5); `deliveries/example-room/` is a small accepted-looking
   delivery to copy from.
3. **Make the proofs** (`python3 tools/build_proofs.py deliveries/<slug>`, see "Proofs" below), refresh the manifest, then **check** it yourself:
   `python3 tools/check_all.py deliveries/<slug> --json` must exit 0 (this also runs `tools/check_submission.py` and `tools/check_proofs.py`).
   `tools/ci/run_checks.sh <slug>` runs exactly what the automatic check runs, including the rebuild of the proofs.
4. **Open a pull request** from your branch against `main`. Fill in the checklist in the pull request template.
5. **Automatic check.** A workflow checks the changed delivery folders (see below). Fix every REQUIRED finding and push again.
6. **Review.** A maintainer reads the delivery. The checks cannot judge quality, ownership or fit, so a delivery that passes can still be
   declined or sent back with notes.
7. **Acceptance is a merge to `main`.** Nothing else counts as acceptance, and no tool takes in a delivery from a branch or a fork.
8. **Ingest** runs afterwards, on the merged commit (see "Ingest"). The commit hash is the provenance of everything it produces.

Only the folder `deliveries/<slug>/` should change in a delivery pull request. One delivery per pull request. A correction after
acceptance is a new pull request with a new version in the same folder (X-50: never edit a delivered version in place; add a new `delivery.version`).

---

<!-- chunk: sub--what-a-delivery-folder-holds | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: What a delivery folder holds | rules: - -->
## What a delivery folder holds

A delivery is an ordinary package (guide 4, section 1) with these differences:

```
deliveries/oak-study/
  delivery.json            the manifest (schemas/manifest.schema.json) plus a `submission` object (schemas/submission.schema.json)
  SHA256SUMS.txt           hashes of every file, as in any package
  ifc/<name>-master.ifc    the master IFC file, when the delivery has a building or room
  items/<itemId>/          furniture, fixtures and hardware as items (guide 3): <itemId>.ifc and <itemId>.item.json
  finishes/                finish schedule, library.json and textures/<set>/ (guide 2)
  previews/                pictures of the work (png or jpg) so a reviewer sees it first
  proofs/                  GLB exports, their validation report, the standard renders and manifest.json (made by tools/build_proofs.py)
  reports/ notes/ tables/  the check reports, the change notes and the room table, as in guide 4
```

`delivery.json` is built with `python3 tools/build_package.py init DIR meta.json --manifest-name delivery.json`; the meta file carries the
`delivery`, `author`, `profile`, `frame`, `provenance`, `licence` and `checks` parts of guide 4, section 3, and the `submission` object:

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `title`, `summary` | what the delivery is, in a sentence |
| `submitter.handle` | the account the pull request is opened from (no personal data is needed) |
| `licence` | `CC-BY-4.0` (the default), or `CC0-1.0` when the delivery says so; the profile lists the licences it takes |
| `profile` | name and version of the profile the delivery was checked against |
| `toolVersions` | the tools and libraries used (this guide set's version, the IFC library) |
| `attestation` | `ownWork`, `mayLicense`, `noRestrictedContent`, all `true` |

Contributed assets are offered under CC BY 4.0 unless the delivery states CC0. By opening the pull request the contributor attests that they
own the work or may license it, and that it contains no restricted third-party content (X-22, X-76).

---

<!-- chunk: sub--proofs | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: Proofs | rules: - -->
## Proofs

Every submitted delivery carries **proofs**: models and pictures that anyone can look at without a modelling program, and rebuild to see that
they are honest. `python3 tools/build_proofs.py deliveries/<slug>` makes all of them from the delivered files, in three steps, and writes
`proofs/manifest.json` (`schemas/proofs.schema.json`, format `proofs/1`):

1. **Export** (`tools/export_glb.py`): `proofs/glb/model.glb` (the whole master IFC as a scene graph: `model` > `level:<name>` >
   `<kind>:<name>#<GlobalId>`), `proofs/glb/components/*.glb` (one per item and per furniture element, covering, fixture or luminaire
   assembly, hardware piece, door and window, exactly the GLB `ingest.py` stores for it) and `proofs/glb/materials/*.glb` (a 2 x 2 swatch of each
   texture set with its maps embedded). Units are metres and the axes are Y up: an IFC point (x, y, z) becomes (x, z, -y). Colours are PBR
   metallic-roughness materials. The files are deterministic and hold no path, time, user or host.
2. **Validate** (`tools/validate_glb.py`): structure (container, indices, accessors, images, materials, scene graph, nothing unused, no URI),
   conventions (units and axis note, generator, size, unit-length normals, tangents with a normal map, node names), the profile's budgets, and
   with `--ifc` each product's bounding box against the IFC file. The Khronos glTF Validator (Apache-2.0, pinned in
   `tools/khronos/package-lock.json`, `npm ci --prefix tools/khronos`) is run as well when it is installed. The report is
   `proofs/reports/glb-validation.json` (`check-report/1`, rule X-80).
3. **Render** (`tools/render.py`), from the GLB files only: a plan for each level (cut at 1.2 m), four interior views for each room kind
   present (kind = the room's `Function` property; the first two rooms of a kind by identifier), four exterior views, and a contact sheet of
   eight turntable frames for every component (four fixed frames for a texture swatch).

The renderer is a software rasteriser in numpy (about 400 lines): no graphics card, display, browser or system library, so the same GLB gives
the same picture on a laptop and on a hosted runner. It draws flat-shaded triangles with a z-buffer, 2 x 2 supersampled, with base colours and
the base colour texture; it does not draw normal maps, metal, roughness, shadows or reflections. The lighting, background, camera and sizes are
fixed conventions, recorded for every picture (`tools/render.py` states them). A headless browser with a bundled viewer library, or Blender, would draw
nicer pictures, but they depend on a graphics stack that differs between machines, so the same file would not give the same picture; the
choice favours reproducibility over beauty. (Tried while choosing: headless Chromium with software WebGL runs here and repeats itself on one machine, but needs a browser, a
vendored viewer library of some hundreds of kilobytes, and gives pixels that depend on the browser and graphics-layer build; Blender is optional
high-quality software that is far larger than this repository and, with a graphics card, differs from machine to machine.) The manifest records, for every GLB, its SHA-256, size and source IFC hash, and for every picture
its path, SHA-256, pixel size, camera, light, the hash of the GLB it was made from and the tool and version.

`python3 tools/check_proofs.py deliveries/<slug>` checks the manifest against the files (X-79), the GLB files against their sources and the
validation report (X-81, X-80), the coverage of the pictures (X-82), the traceability of each picture to a delivered GLB (X-83), the size limits
(X-84) and the metadata of every image and GLB (X-85); with `--reproduce` it also rebuilds the GLB files, compares the bytes, re-renders every
picture from the delivered GLB and compares it within `proofs.renderTolerance` (X-86). Where the toolchain is not available it says so (an
`info` finding) and skips; it never reports a skipped check as passed. Make the proofs again after any change to an IFC file, item or texture set.

---

<!-- chunk: sub--limits | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: Limits | rules: - -->
## Limits

Defaults, all parameters of the profile (`submission` and `proofs` groups, see `07-profile-parameters.md`): at most 600 files (proofs add a GLB and a sheet for every component; it was 200 before 2.3.0), 25 MiB per file, 100 MiB per
delivery; file types ifc, glb, png, jpg, json, md, csv and txt only (csv and txt exist because the room table and `SHA256SUMS.txt` need them);
no program, script, archive or executable file mode; no symbolic links; relative, portable, case-unique paths of at most 200 characters; images of
at most 64 million pixels; renders of at least 256 and at most about 2 million pixels and 3 MiB, and `proofs/` of at most 64 MiB. A consumer that accepts submissions can set other values in its own profile.

---

<!-- chunk: sub--the-automatic-check | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: The automatic check | rules: - -->
## The automatic check

`.github/workflows/check-delivery.yml` (a copy of the same steps without any workflow system is `tools/ci/run_checks.sh`) runs on pull requests
that touch `deliveries/**`. It installs the pinned requirements (`tools/requirements-ci.txt`), then for each changed delivery runs
`check_submission.py` and `check_all.py` under `profiles/default.json`, and again under `profiles/<name>.json` when `delivery.json` names a profile
that exists there; once under the default profile it also runs `check_proofs.py --reproduce` (it rebuilds the proofs on the runner, which has no graphics card) and
`validate_glb.py` with the pinned Khronos glTF Validator (installed by `npm ci`, no secret needed). It uploads the JSON reports as an artifact, writes a summary to the run, and fails on any REQUIRED finding.

Pull requests from forks run with a read-only token and no secrets, and the workflow never uses `pull_request_target`. A first-time
contributor's run may wait until a maintainer approves it. A fork's token cannot write comments, so the result is the run summary and the
artifact; for pull requests from branches of this repository the workflow also posts the summary as a comment.

---

<!-- chunk: sub--ingest | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: Ingest | rules: - -->
## Ingest

`python3 tools/ingest.py deliveries/<slug> --commit <merged commit hash> --out <output folder>` is run by a maintainer or an automation, on a
checkout of the merged commit of `main` (`--require-ancestor-of origin/main` makes it refuse anything else). It never uploads and uses no
network. In order, it:

1. copies the delivery (plain files only) to a temporary folder, with a time limit (`submission.ingestMaxSeconds`) and an optional memory limit;
2. re-runs `check_submission.py` and `check_all.py` on the copy (the latter includes the stored-file checks of the proofs), and refuses on any REQUIRED finding;
3. splits the delivery into **components**: each item under `items/`; from the master IFC each furniture element, covering (wall, floor or
   ceiling), fixture or luminaire assembly, hardware piece, door and window; each texture set as a material set;
4. exports each geometry component as a binary glTF (GLB, units metres, Y up) and reads it back to verify it;
5. stores every file as `blobs/sha256/<hash>.<ext>`; identical bytes (for example a table in `items/` and the same table in the master, or the
   same part in two deliveries) are stored once;
6. compares the contributor's proofs with a fresh export from the delivered files (GLB hashes, render hashes, and that every component GLB of the
   ingest is among the proofs) and reports any mismatch in the result; the ingest result stays authoritative and nothing is refused for it. Each
   component links the contact sheet of its GLB (`proof-render` file), and the delivery record lists every render and the GLB files;
7. writes `catalogue/index.json` (one entry per distinct component, with every occurrence), `catalogue/deliveries/<slug>@<commit12>.json`
   and the handoff manifest `handoff/<slug>@<commit12>.json`, shaped by `schemas/catalogue.schema.json`.

Each component carries: kind and category; dimensions and bounds; the pivot (items keep the pivot their description declares, master elements are
moved to the centre of their footprint at their lowest point); anchors; the material references that link surface colours to the finish schedule and
to the material-set components; and, per occurrence, the delivery slug, commit hash, submitter, licence, source path and IFC identifier, and its
placement in the building file. The output depends only on the delivery bytes and the commit hash, so a second run gives the same bytes. `--dry-run` shows what
would be stored and what the output folder already holds, and writes nothing.

The handoff manifest lists the blobs to publish and the components with their files, licences and submitters. Publishing them anywhere is a
separate step owned by whoever runs the catalogue; this repository defines no destination.

Limits of this version: the renders show base colours and one texture (no normal maps, metal or roughness); a texture set is shown as a swatch, not on a wall; components from the master IFC are exported as GLB only (no per-component IFC file; item components also keep their source
IFC); walls, slabs, stairs and roofs are not components, only furnishing, coverings, fixtures, hardware, doors and windows; rotations are recorded
as an angle about the vertical axis; textures are carried as material sets and are not baked into the GLB.

---

<!-- chunk: sub--for-agents | source: 08-submissions-and-ingest.md | title: For agents | rules: - -->
## For agents

Harness-neutral steps; each command exits non-zero on failure. Replace `UPSTREAM` with the repository you were asked to contribute to.

```
gh repo fork UPSTREAM --clone --default-branch-only        # your fork, cloned; or fork in the web page
cd REPO && git checkout -b delivery-SLUG
pip install -r tools/requirements.txt
# build deliveries/SLUG/ (skills/submit-delivery/SKILL.md), then:
python3 tools/build_proofs.py deliveries/SLUG                         # GLB files, validation report, renders, manifest; then refresh delivery.json
python3 tools/check_all.py deliveries/SLUG --json --out report.json   # exit 0 required
git add deliveries/SLUG && git commit -m "feat(deliveries): add SLUG" -m "What it is and what it was checked against."
git push -u origin delivery-SLUG
gh pr create --repo UPSTREAM --base main --title "Delivery: SLUG" --body-file .github/pull_request_template.md
```

Fill in the checklist honestly; do not tick the attestation boxes unless they are true, and do not set `attestation` fields to `true` for work you
cannot vouch for. Never edit tools, profiles or schemas in a delivery pull request. Stop and report if the same REQUIRED finding remains after
three runs (`REPAIR-LOOP.md`).

---

<!-- chunk: repair--introduction | source: REPAIR-LOOP.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# Repair loop

How to get a deliverable to zero REQUIRED findings. The same loop works for a building, a material library, a
furniture library and a package. It needs only the tools in `tools/`; no network and no service.

---

<!-- chunk: repair--the-loop | source: REPAIR-LOOP.md | title: The loop | rules: - -->
## The loop

1. **Run** one command for the deliverable, printing JSON:

   ```
   python3 tools/check_all.py PATH --json --out report.json
   ```

   (`PATH` is a master `.ifc` file, a folder with `finishes/`, a folder with `items/`, or a package folder with
   `manifest.json`. Add `--profile PROFILE.json` for a building so the frame, identifiers and volumes are checked.)
2. **Read** the report. Look at `result`, `exitCode` and `summary.requiredFailures` first. Then list the findings
   whose `status` is `fail`: each has `rule`, `message`, `location.element` (a `GlobalId`, when one product is
   concerned), `location.file` and `fix_hint`. For more on a rule, open its entry in `rules.json` (`statement`,
   `rationale`, `examples`, `related`).
3. **Fix** the source of the deliverable (the model, the schedule, the item, the package inputs), not the report.
   Fix the lowest-numbered structural findings first (`B-01` to `B-06`, `B-13`, `B-20` to `B-26`): later findings often
   disappear with them. Make one kind of change at a time.
4. **Rebuild** whatever the fix touched (re-export the IFC, rebuild the manifest with `build_package.py init`).
5. **Rerun** step 1 and compare. Repeat until `summary.requiredFailures` is 0 and the exit code is 0.

Then look at `warn` findings (RECOMMENDED rules). Fix the ones whose `fix_hint` is cheap; list the rest in
`notes/open-points.md`.

---

<!-- chunk: repair--report-fields | source: REPAIR-LOOP.md | title: Report fields | rules: - -->
## Report fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `result` | `pass`, `fail` or `error` |
| `exitCode` | `0` no REQUIRED rule failed; `1` at least one did; `2` wrong command line; `3` an input could not be read |
| `summary` | counts: `requiredFailures`, `recommendedWarnings`, `passes`, `info` |
| `findings[].id` | stable: the rule id, then a short hash of rule, file, element and message; the same problem keeps the same id between runs |
| `findings[].status` | `pass`, `info`, `warn` (RECOMMENDED not met) or `fail` (REQUIRED not met) |
| `findings[].fix_hint` | what to change, present on `warn` and `fail` |
| `reports[]` | the full report of each tool that `check_all.py` ran |

To list only what must be fixed, read the file with any JSON tool, for example:

```
python3 -c "import json;r=json.load(open('report.json'));[print(f['rule'],f['location'],f['message'],'->',f['fix_hint']) for f in r['findings'] if f['status']=='fail']"
```

---

<!-- chunk: repair--stop-conditions | source: REPAIR-LOOP.md | title: Stop conditions | rules: - -->
## Stop conditions

Stop and report instead of looping when any of these holds:

* The same finding `id` is still present after three runs in a row. Report the finding, what you changed, and why you
  think it did not help.
* The exit code is `3`, or `result` is `error`. Fix the path or the missing input; this is not a rule failure.
* A fix needs information that is not in the profile or the files (an `Occupant` string, a level offset, a licence
  statement, the assigned entity-number start). Ask the person who gave you the profile; do not invent it.
* More than ten runs without the number of REQUIRED failures going down.
* A finding seems wrong. Say which rule and element, and what you measured. Do not work around it.

---

<!-- chunk: repair--never-do-these-to-get-a-pass | source: REPAIR-LOOP.md | title: Never do these to get a pass | rules: - -->
## Never do these to get a pass

* Edit a report, change a rule level, delete a check, or edit a tool to hide a finding.
* Change a value only to satisfy the checker when it makes the model less true (for example, widening a door in
  the file while the drawing says otherwise).
* Delete the element that is flagged without saying so in `notes/changes.md`.
* Run the checker on a different file than the one you deliver (rule `X-40` ties the report to the file by hash).

---

<!-- chunk: repair--worked-mini-loop | source: REPAIR-LOOP.md | title: Worked mini-loop | rules: - -->
## Worked mini-loop

Run 1 prints a failure:

```
{ "rule": "B-42", "status": "fail", "location": {"element": "3Z2k6lcTnJFPCzw1CFlWEi"},
  "message": "doorway Entrance door is blocked at 0.6 m by Work table, 1.6 m",
  "fix_hint": "Make the opening at least 1.9 m high and remove anything (sill, bar, furniture) that crosses the doorway centre line." }
```

Fix: move the table out of the doorway and re-export. Run 2 shows `summary.requiredFailures` 0 and exit code 0. Then
rebuild the manifest (`python3 tools/build_package.py init PACKAGE_DIR package-meta.json`), run
`python3 tools/check_all.py PACKAGE_DIR --json`, and deliver.

---

<!-- chunk: review--introduction | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: Introduction | rules: - -->
<!-- SPDX-License-Identifier: CC-BY-4.0 -->
# Environment review and asynchronous handoff

This procedure supplements guides 1–4. It adds review guidance, not new default
rule levels. The consumer's profile supplies tolerances, clearance, camera,
device and performance targets. A valid file can still depict a poor environment.

---

<!-- chunk: review--1-agree-the-work-and-pin-its-inputs | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: 1. Agree the work and pin its inputs | rules: - -->
## 1. Agree the work and pin its inputs

Assign one owner per editable source or shared exporter. Separate model author,
material author, consumer integration and independent review where practical.
Work on branches; do not overwrite an accepted delivery or another worker's
candidate. Independent rooms and assets can proceed in parallel. Serialize
changes to shared generators, material contracts and publication manifests.

Record the guide/profile versions and hashes, source commit, editable sources,
dependencies, exact build commands, units and coordinate transform. Distinguish
the canonical model hash from an optimized consumer model hash. A screenshot
needs the latter, its material/lightmap assets, renderer version and camera.
Use `templates/environment-handoff.template.json` for a resumable work record.
Reference the evidence manifest and frozen render-input manifest by path and hash;
they bind captures to model, pose, lightmaps, renderer modules, cameras, method and
diagnostic limits. Include those files in the portable handoff.

Deliver relative paths and immutable artifact addresses that collaborators can
access. A working-machine path or symlink alone is not a handoff. Keep rights,
font/texture dependencies, procedural seeds and storage requirements with sources.
Never include credentials or depend on a contributor's running browser session.

---

<!-- chunk: review--2-check-construction-and-usable-space-before-mul | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: 2. Check construction and usable space before multiplying media | rules: - -->
## 2. Check construction and usable space before multiplying media

Inventory every authored room, exterior and connection. Review a complete set
of directions and upward/downward joins, then relevant closeups. A few attractive
hero views do not prove room coverage. List places not inspected and why.

Inspect openings, wall/roof/bay joins, thresholds, chimney bores and flashing,
hardware attachment, furniture clearances, support contacts and actual object
orientation. Check props against the real support surface, not an assumed floor
height. Model masonry bonds and corner returns when joints must align.

Verify the requested open-door state against actual fixed surfaces and other
open leaves. “Open” is not synonymous with “passable.” Do not hide a blocking
leaf, enlarge a clearance result, or rotate a leaf into a wall to obtain a pass.
Preserve the neutral rig and record hinge, parts and applied pose exactly once.

Use actual finished-floor geometry for steps, decks and ramps. Semantic level
labels and large furniture bounding boxes can misrepresent walkable space.
Evaluate the consumer's body clearance and all required connections; compute
connectivity again after stair/threshold repairs. A room viewpoint should lie on
an accessible component, not a comfortable-looking isolated patch behind furniture.
Separate photographic compositions from natural standing/entry viewpoints.
Verify the actual projection matrix, sensor convention and aspect ratio. A nominal
lens label is insufficient if the consumer ignores it or applies a default field
of view; qualify affected historical captures rather than silently relabeling them.

---

<!-- chunk: review--3-review-material-authoring-and-exported-appeara | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: 3. Review material authoring and exported appearance separately | rules: - -->
## 3. Review material authoring and exported appearance separately

Name the intended surface: paint, wood species, metal/coating, plaster, glass,
fabric, stone, foliage. A solid painted finish is often correct; do not substitute
a generic timber or noise texture merely because the exporter has one available.

Check UV orientation, real scale, repetition and seams at corners and close range.
Inspect color, normal, roughness, metallic, emission and optical properties after
export and import into the intended consumer. Retain material identity through
batching. Inspect winding and authored normals on both sides of foliage. For
closed shells, check outward orientation as well as surface positions; preserve
intentional single-sided geometry under the profile's sidedness convention. Texture-cache keys must include settings that change the resulting material.

Alpha coverage alone does not establish believable clear glass. Preserve the
source's intended transmission, index of refraction and roughness using supported
properties; keep mirror and painted/opaque surfaces distinct. Record unsupported
features. Do not silently replace materials by name in a proof renderer: that can
make a broken export appear correct. Label diagnostic fill lights and substitutions;
they cannot prove the unmodified consumer's appearance.

---

<!-- chunk: review--4-prove-the-lighting-and-renderer-contract | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: 4. Prove the lighting and renderer contract | rules: - -->
## 4. Prove the lighting and renderer contract

Document whether diffuse direct/indirect illumination is baked or evaluated at
runtime. Avoid counting both. Preserve source UVs separately from lightmap UVs;
verify geometry identity, UV coverage, overlap, receivers and gutters after optimization.

When filtering Monte Carlo noise, keep contact/direct shadow detail out of an
indirect-light smoothing operation. Filter independent atlas charts independently.
Specify linear versus display-encoded values, range/scale, texture channels and
tone mapping. Check pixel values after delivery encoding: lossy image coding can
introduce colored blocks into unrelated atlas islands. An attractive source render
does not prove an optimized map or a different renderer. Isolate albedo, direct
and indirect illumination before changing textures or adding fill to conceal a
lighting defect. Record sampling, path-depth, glossy-blur and clamping settings:
noise controls can change transmitted energy, and more samples alone may not
remove that bias. Keep raw passes and compare bounded transport fixtures against
an appropriate physical reference; record convergence limits explicitly.

Review actual consumer views of dark rooms, bright windows, foliage backsides,
glass, metals and contact shadows. A changed sky must agree with the baked light's
direction and color convention. Record dark, noisy or implausible results as open
findings; do not declare the pipeline finished because its scripts exited successfully.

---

<!-- chunk: review--5-package-evidence-that-another-contributor-can | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: 5. Package evidence that another contributor can continue | rules: - -->
## 5. Package evidence that another contributor can continue

For each finding record severity, affected objects/rooms, observation, artifact
hashes, correction owner, attempted fix and the matching verification view. Keep
baseline and candidate evidence separate. A changed artifact invalidates its old
acceptance; record a superseding decision rather than editing away adverse evidence.

| Change | Evidence to revisit |
|---|---|
| Geometry or pose | Collision/support, connectivity, room stops, UVs, bake, media and consumer integration |
| Materials or source UVs | Export/import parity, relevant bake contributions, optical closeups and media |
| Renderer, sky or lighting | Matched views, affected media and device measurements |
| Encoding/optimization | Decoded pixels/surfaces, attribute retention and consumer views |
| Labels or publication only | Affected links, accessibility, asset integrity and deployed behavior |

Reuse a prior geometry/navigation result for a material-only revision only when
an explicit equivalence check proves unchanged relevant geometry and poses. A
matching vertex count is insufficient; changed triangle diagonals can matter.

Record reviewer independence and limits. Schema validation, image existence,
reproducibility and visual acceptance are separate results. A diagnostic render,
software renderer or emulated phone must not be represented as a physical-device test.
Measure actual transfer, first usable frame, frame times and repeated-entry resource
cleanup. Optimize from evidence without hiding quality loss or inventing a universal limit.

---

<!-- chunk: review--6-resume-and-improve | source: 09-environment-review-and-handoff.md | title: 6. Resume and improve | rules: - -->
## 6. Resume and improve

The receiving contributor verifies artifact hashes, reads open findings and runs
the recorded next command. Record the output revision, decisions and remaining
work in the handoff; attach readable contact sheets and exact evidence files.
Release owned processes and scratch storage without deleting editable masters.
Do not claim an old job is running without checking its real handle.

When a defect escapes the process, add its general cause, a reproducible example
and a source/export/review check to the appropriate guide or tool. Fix the shared
recipe as well as the particular asset. Acceptance remains the receiving party's
explicit, revision-bound decision under guide 4.

---
